newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 31.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- MERRILL MAN LANDS THREE MILLION STG BONUS PAY

Connie Voldstad, the London-based executive who runs American investment bank Merrill Lynch's debt market division, will be paid a bonus of $5 million. Also 20 of his colleagues in corporate finance, bonds and derivatives departments are expected to receive payments of about $1 million each. Despite the 31 percent rise in Merrill's annual profits to a record $1.6 billion expectations of bonus payments had not been high.
-- BROKER IS BLAMED AS FARNELL PRICE DIPS

Chief executive of Premier Farnell, Howard Poulson, has accused the company's stockbroker BZW of mishandling the group's profits warning late on Wednesday. Shares in the electronics distributor have fallen to 520 pence. Poulson said he was appalled by the collapse and claimed that profits would miss market forecasts by up to eight percent and had been "badly mismanaged".
-- EVERSHOT ON LINE FOR BONANZA

Another huge windfall from rail privatisation will come with the 600 million stg takeover of Evershot, the train leasing group, by HSBC Holdings. The key to the windfalls will be how much of Evershot's 510 million stg debt, from last January, has been paid down. Paying off debt increases Evershot's value as the company's structure means a 10 percent rise in worth triggers a leap in the value of ordinary equity. HSBC could boost the total by issuing bonds, repayable from leasing revenue.
THE TIMES
-- INSTITUTE CUTS PREDICTION ON GROWTH

The National Institute of Economic and Social Research, an influential economic research group, has cut its growth forecast for this year, saying that the pound is hampering GDP growth while keeping the lid on inflation. The group predicts that GDP will rise just 2.5 percent in 1997 compared with its last forecast of 3.4 percent. The group also forecasts that inflation will fall to 2.1 percent in 1997, below the Government's target level of 2.5 percent, and will remain subdued for a further two years.
-- YORKSHIRE PAYBACK PROPOSAL ATTACKED

Yorkshire Water have announced plans to return 145 million stg to shareholders. Consumer groups, Consumers' Association and Waterwatch, have demanded intervention from the regulator for fresh price caps on the company because there is no rebate or price reduction for customers. Yorkshire faced problems during the 1995 drought and was subsequently penalised with a price freeze and fine.
-- SFA IMPOSES BAN ON BARINGS 'WHISTLEBLOWER'

Ian Hopkins, the former head of group treasury and risk at Barings, has been barred by the Securities and Futures Authority from holding a senior post in the City for up to three years. He is thought to have been the only executive at the bank to raise concerns over Nick Leeson's dealings on the Far East money markets. He has been called a 'whistleblower' for memos he wrote and issues he raised at meetings over Leeson's trading.
THE GUARDIAN
-- DTI URGED TO INVESTIGATE WILLIAM COOK SHARE DEALINGS

The DTI has been asked to open an insider dealing inquiry into the Sheffield steel castings group, William Cook, which has been at the centre of takeover battles. The request centres on the decision to buy back 5.5 percent of its own shares at the end of October, and it is believed it comes from one of Triplex's City supporters, the rival steel group which issued a bid attack six weeks later. William Cook deny knowledge of the move and say the share repurchase was legitimate.
-- AUDITOR
CLAIMS BCCI VICTORY

Ernst and Young and Deloitte and Touche, two of Britain's largest accountancy firms, are facing major disagreements after a judge threw out $1.8 billion worth of claims relating to the collapse of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International. Ernst and Young, former auditor of part of BCCI, claimed victory saying it would be able to dismiss the rest of the claims against it. Deloitte and Touche, liquidator of the bank, said its main $1.7 billion claim against Ernst still stood and would be pursued.
-- TOYOTA PUTS BRAKES ON INVESTMENT ROW

President of Toyota, Hiroshi Okuda, has been forced to issue a statement saying that nothing had been decided about future investment in Europe. He said that Britain's commitment to EMU would be only one factor in any investment decision. This is an attempt to extricate Toyota from a pre-election row about the UK's commitment to economic and monetary union. However, truckmaker Iveco has provoked renewed concerns about job losses when it announced a review of its manufacturing capabilities in Europe.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- FOOTBALL CLUBS MAY INVEST IN FOREIGN TEAMS

Top British football clubs are likely to anger football fans and please investors by examining ways of taking cross- shareholding in leading continental teams. Having European clubs owning shares in each other is intended to limit the risk to investors of backing just one club and could pave the way for a series of marketing, merchandising and television deals binding them together. This comes as more European clubs prepare to join British clubs by going public.
-- NADIR AIDE FREED PENDING APPEAL

Former aide to Asil Nadir, the fugitive Polly Peck tycoon, Elizabeth Forsyth, has been released from prison after the appeal court ruled her sentence may have been too harsh. She was jailed for five years last March for laundering 400,000 stg. An appeal hearing today may take evidence from Nadir via a video link or recording. Nadir recruited Forsyth when she was working for Citibank and put her in charge of his personal company, South Audley Management, which administered the Nadir family interests.
-- SAUDIS POISED TO SIGN $20 BILLION LOCKHEED DEAL

Saudi Arabia is set to sign a deal with Lockheed Martin, the US plane-maker, to buy 100 F-16 fighter jets worth $20 billion. The agreement could shift the focus of Saudi Arabia's vast defence spending programme from the UK to the US. A spokesman for British Aerospace declined to comment on the deal and observers say it could strengthen the hand of Lockheed Martin in the Middle East while European governments continue to wrangle over the 40 billion stg Eurofighter project.
